headline: Six years a food-delivery rider, just licensed to fly drones within visual line of sight, now loading, launching and catching delivery drones on a landing pad on a mall roof in Nanshan, Shenzhen
unit: A drone instant-delivery company in Nanshan, Shenzhen, running a dozen-odd routes from malls to parks, office towers and pickup lockers by the sea
education: Secondary vocational school (auto repair), later a civil drone pilot license (visual line of sight)
level: You can do pre-flight checks, swap batteries, hang the cargo box, and launch and catch drones on the pad by the manual. On the ground control station you can only watch, not edit a route, and you haven't taken the beyond-visual-line-of-sight license yet
intro: You delivered food for six years, and you know the back door of every office tower in Nanshan. Last winter you saw a drone land on a pickup locker in a park, and the next day you signed up for a license course. Now you stand on a landing pad on a mall roof, waiting for drones to come back one after another. As of today, the things you deliver no longer travel by road.
salary_note: Estimate: a drone delivery operations job in Shenzhen, base pay plus a per-flight bonus, runs about twenty percent above the national figure. In typhoon and rainy-season months, with many flights grounded, take-home pay drops noticeably.

facts.label: Landing-Pad Operator / Drone Test Pilot (current level)
facts.value: 0-1 years, ¥5,270–7,750 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: Next level up
facts.value: Low-Altitude Logistics Operator (Drone Logistics Operator) (1-3 years)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Opening a new delivery route and flying the trials

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Pre-flight checks, loading and launch for one delivery flight

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 1 related job listing nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: The wind on the roof is stronger than on the street. First you check wind speed on your phone: six meters a second, flyable. You carry the batteries charged overnight out of the charging cabinet one by one, checking temperature and cycle count.
Pre-flight checks. You turn each propeller blade, feel for cracks, press the cargo box latches, and tick the checklist on your tablet item by item.

The first order comes in: four cups of fruit tea from a tea shop downstairs, to the pickup locker in Talent Park. You lock the cups into a spill-proof tray, close the cargo box, step back behind the yellow line and report: ready to launch.
Lunch rush, one drone landing after another. You catch, pull the empty box, swap the battery, hang the next order. In your ears is the hum of rotors, and your hands get faster and faster.

You eat a meal from the mall's staff canteen in the stairwell. Your phone buzzes: the rider group chat from your old delivery station, someone asking which business district has the most orders today.
As one drone comes down it wobbles, and a vibration alert pops up on the ground station. By the rules you ground it, take photos, fill in a fault ticket and hand it to maintenance.
Fog rolls in by the sea, and dispatch grounds the two routes to the waterfront. You hand the waiting orders to riders on the ground and call the customers one by one to explain.

Before you clock off you plug every battery back into the charging cabinet, wipe the blades clean, and write today's flight count and one vibration alert in the handover book. By the time you go downstairs the mall is about to close.

ladder.title: Landing-Pad Operator / Drone Test Pilot
ladder.focus: Holding a visual-line-of-sight license, handle loading and handover at the landing pad, route testing and data collection. Former delivery riders and others switching careers start here.

ladder.title: Low-Altitude Logistics Operator (Drone Logistics Operator)
ladder.focus: Holding a beyond-visual-line-of-sight license, fly delivery routes independently, doing weather assessment, ground control station operation and emergency handling.

ladder.title: Remote Pilot in Command / Route Operations Supervisor
ladder.focus: Responsible for multi-aircraft monitoring, route development and operating metrics.

ladder.title: Low-Altitude Logistics Dispatch / Operations Manager
ladder.focus: Run the operations center, certification and compliance, training and safety.

ladder.title: Head of Low-Altitude Logistics Network
ladder.focus: Regional route network planning and liaison with government and businesses.

ai_tasks.name: Pre-flight checks, loading and launch for one delivery flight
ai_tasks.how: AI can check the order automatically, read battery and weather data, work out whether the payload is over limit and recommend whether to launch. A person on site confirms the airframe's condition, that the cargo is secured and that the area around the pad is safe, and makes the final call to launch.

ai_tasks.name: Monitoring several flights remotely and handling lost-link alerts
ai_tasks.how: AI can watch many routes at once, spot link anomalies automatically and push the response steps from the playbook. A person decides whether an alert is real, whether to return or make a forced landing, and answers for the outcome.

ai_tasks.name: Opening a new delivery route and flying the trials
ai_tasks.how: AI can help read maps, draft a route and organize the application documents. But landing sites in the mountains have to be surveyed in person, there are village clinics and villagers to talk to and airspace authorities to deal with, and the judgment and responsibility during trial flights are a person's to carry.

ai_tasks.name: Daily maintenance and battery management
ai_tasks.how: AI can predict the life of wearing parts from flight data, track battery cycles and remind you when to replace and charge. A person has to inspect the airframe by hand, take parts off and put them on, catch odd noises and cracks the data can't see, and sign off the aircraft as airworthy.

ai_tasks.name: Grounding flights in high wind and rearranging orders
ai_tasks.how: AI can compare wind forecasts against the aircraft's limits, prompt a grounding, and draft a plan to reschedule or switch to ground delivery. A person weighs the actual conditions on site, makes the call to ground, and coordinates special orders with dispatch and customers.

ai_tasks.name: Handling the annual operating certification review and insurance renewal
ai_tasks.how: AI can pretty much assemble the licenses, flight records and certification documents, generate the review forms, compare insurance terms and flag expiry dates. A person only needs to spot-check that the materials are genuine and complete, then sign and submit.

events.e_first_flight: The first time you launch on your own, you watch the drone climb, turn and clear the roof of the building opposite. You stand on the roof a long while, waiting for it to become a small returning dot on the ground station.
events.e_rider_days: From the roof you watch riders below threading through traffic, and think of the afternoon you were held up at one red light and docked pay for a bad review. Now you stand up here, under the same sun.
events.e_typhoon: A typhoon is coming, and the whole city is grounded for three days. You and your coworkers stow the drones one by one in the hangar and strap down the cargo boxes and charging cabinets. Your bonus that month is almost zero.
events.e_heat: The roof in August, the concrete hot enough to burn through your shoes. You drink six bottles of water a day, the back of your uniform dries and soaks again, and at night there's a red ring around your neck.
events.e_kid: By the pickup locker in the park, a little boy comes every weekend to wait for the drones to land. One day his mother comes over and asks you: for a job like this, what should he study?
events.e_bvlos: You pass the beyond-visual-line-of-sight license and sit at the monitoring desk for the first time, watching three routes at once. Little drones weave between the towers on the screen, and your palms are soaked.
events.e_link_loss: Halfway along a route a drone loses its link for a dozen seconds and hovers automatically, as the playbook says. You count the seconds on the screen. Only when the signal returns do you realize you've been holding your breath.
events.e_complaint: A bowl of rice noodle soup arrives half spilled, and the customer posts a video saying drone delivery is a gimmick. The company has you redesign the tray, and you go through three versions.
events.e_rain_season: The muggy 'return south' damp of spring and then thunderstorm season: in one month there are a dozen days of switching back and forth between grounding and resuming. Your phone is full of weather radar, and you check it once more before bed.
events.e_love: A clerk from the bookshop in the mall comes up to the roof every noon for some air. You teach her which way up a propeller goes, and she leaves you a book about weather.
events.e_medical: The company takes on a route carrying blood samples between hospitals. On your first run of that route, the cargo box holds not milk tea but a sealed cold box. You watch its temperature every second.
events.e_ai_dispatch: The dispatch system gets AI: it schedules flights, calculates battery, and routes around temporary no-fly zones on its own, and one person can watch ten drones instead of three. Your job changes from watching the drones to watching it.
events.e_forced_landing: A drone's motor fails and, per the playbook, it puts down in a strip of landscaping without touching anyone. It takes you twenty minutes to find it. Two blades are broken, and somehow the cake in the cargo box isn't even crooked.
events.e_wedding: You go home to Zhanjiang for the wedding. Your younger cousin flies a toy drone at the banquet and hits a lantern, and the whole room looks at you and laughs.
events.e_policy: The city issues new rules for low-altitude flight, and approving routes and building landing sites finally have a clear process. The company files for twenty new routes at once, and there aren't enough people.
events.e_baby: Your daughter is born. The first toy you buy her is a little plastic airplane, and all she does is bang it against the crib rails.
events.e_rent: The landlord raises the rent, and you move to an urban village farther out in Bao'an. The commute is forty minutes longer, and on the metro you often fall asleep standing up.
events.e_noise: Residents of a housing estate jointly complain that a route is too noisy and demand it be moved. You go to three meetings at the estate, stand below the buildings with a decibel meter, and in the end move the route over the river channel.
events.e_ai_pilot: The new generation of drones takes off, avoids obstacles and lands on its own, and the landing pad no longer needs someone standing by to launch. The roof used to have a dozen people; now three are left, all watching screens.
events.e_back: The back injury from your riding days flares up again, on top of years sitting all day at the monitoring desk. You go for massage, and the therapist says your back is ten years older than you are.
events.e_old_rider: You interview a new pilot, and across the table is a rider from your old station. He says he got the license too. Looking at his résumé, you think of the notes you took in your own license course.
events.e_network: The map you drew of the low-altitude delivery network for the Greater Bay Area hangs on the wall of the company meeting room: more than forty landing sites, a dozen of which you scouted on foot yourself.

c_bvlos.title: Get the beyond-visual-line-of-sight license and become a Low-Altitude Logistics Operator
c_bvlos.situation: Everyone on the pad knows that only with the beyond-visual-line-of-sight license can you sit at the monitoring desk and fly routes on your own, and your bonus doubles. The course costs over ¥10,000, two months of theory and practical, and you can only go on your days off.

options.label: Pay for the course
options.result: You hand over a big chunk of what you've saved these past few years. In the exam, the simulated lost-link test, you pass on the first try.

options.label: Work another year and save up
options.result: You decide not to sign up yet and take extra shifts. Two people who started with you get licensed and move to the monitoring desk, and you're still catching drones on the roof.

c_back_to_rider.title: Go back to delivering food
c_back_to_rider.situation: Base pay on the pad isn't high, and there are a lot of grounded days. The manager of your old delivery station calls: order volume is big now, come back and run a zone, and you'll make thirty percent more than now.

options.label: Go back to riding
options.result: You take off the landing pad's reflective vest and put that helmet back on.
options.end: You went back to the road, weaving through traffic. Now and then at a red light you look up, see a drone cross overhead, and watch it a little longer.

options.label: Stay on the roof
options.result: You say you'll think about it. As you hang up a drone is just landing, and you go over to catch it.

options.label: Work the roof by day and ride two more hours at night
options.result: After clocking off you get on your e-bike and deliver for two more hours, making ¥2,000 more a month, and you fall straight asleep when you get back to your rented room.

c_maintenance.title: Learn aircraft maintenance on the side
c_maintenance.situation: The maintenance crew is short-handed and asks if you want to learn repairs on the side: swapping motors and props, checking sensors, reading the vibration curves in the flight logs. Once you know it, you won't have to wait when a drone breaks, but every day you'll clock off two hours later.

options.label: Learn it and stay two hours later
options.result: You spend half a year taking drones apart in the hangar, the grease never quite washing off your hands. Later, whenever a drone sounds off, you can tell which motor it is just by listening.

options.label: Don't; focus on flying
options.result: You say flying the routes well is enough. The maintenance crew is perfectly polite to you, and broken drones still have to wait.

c_mountain.title: Go open new routes in the mountains
c_mountain.situation: The company has won a project for parcel and medicine delivery in the mountains of northern Guangdong. They need someone to survey landing sites, talk to village clinics and apply to the airspace authorities: six months away, with good allowances. You'd get to open a route on your own, a long way from home.

options.label: Go to the mountains
options.result: You spend six months in the mountains, and one route cuts the trip from a village clinic to the township hospital from an hour to twelve minutes. The village doctor treats you to a night of drinking.

options.label: Stay in Shenzhen
options.result: You say your family needs you. The coworker who goes comes back several shades darker, and gets promoted faster than you.

c_captain.title: Compete for Remote Pilot in Command / Route Operations Supervisor
c_captain.situation: The operations center is promoting a remote pilot in command to oversee multi-aircraft monitoring, open new routes and watch on-time and incident rates. To compete you present your flight record and a route development plan, and explain the closest call you've ever handled.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: You talk about those dozen seconds of lost link, from the numbers on the screen to every step of the playbook. A panelist asks how your plan deals with wind shear, and you answer in detail.

options.label: Fly two more years
options.result: You feel you're not quite there, and don't apply. The new pilot in command is someone you trained, and when he does the roster he always saves you the good routes.

c_ai_ops.title: Learn to review AI dispatch and route plans
c_ai_ops.situation: The company is building a human-machine dispatch desk: AI proposes flights and routes, and people review them and set the emergency procedures. Your supervisor wants you there, which means learning the data dashboards and writing response rules. Some say that's babysitting a machine.

options.label: Go to the dispatch desk
options.result: You become the best at catching AI's mistakes: which route it calculates the wind too optimistically for, which time slot it overloads. You can spot them at a glance.

options.label: Stick to flying
options.result: You say you're a pilot, not someone who watches charts. The AI schedules better and better, and when the weather turns strange, people still come ask you whether to fly.

c_instructor.title: Become a drone instructor at a training school
c_instructor.situation: The training school where you got your license comes looking for you: people are lining up to get licensed now, and they're short of instructors with real delivery experience. You'd no longer have to watch for typhoons and thunderstorms, you'd teach weekend classes, and the pay is about the same.

options.label: Become an instructor
options.result: You pass the instructor certification, and your first lesson is about the day you first launched on your own.
options.end: You became a drone instructor, watching batch after batch of students lift drones off the training field and set them down. You always tell them: check the wind first, then the sky, and last of all yourself.

options.label: Stay in operations
options.result: You say the routes aren't all open yet. The man from the school says you're welcome anytime, and you save his number.

c_ops_manager.title: Take on Low-Altitude Logistics Dispatch / Operations Manager
c_ops_manager.situation: The company is building a new operations center in Qianhai: forty-odd people, over a hundred drones, all the certification reviews and insurance. The boss asks whether you'll take it. Taking it means reports, regulators and incident reports, and rarely touching a drone again.

options.label: Take the operations center
options.result: You start running morning meetings, reading safety reports and visiting regulators, a stack of certification documents on your desk. The last time you launched a drone yourself was three months ago.

options.label: You'd rather manage routes
options.result: You turn it down, saying you're better on the front line. The new manager arrives, and when a route is hard to open, he still comes to you.

c_hometown.title: Go home to Zhanjiang to fly crop-spraying drones
c_hometown.situation: A cousin back home has started a crop-spraying crew for sugarcane fields and orchards, and needs someone who knows drones and can lead people. The license carries over, the money isn't much less than Shenzhen, and in the busy season you work around the clock, in the slack season you're home.

options.label: Go home
options.result: You give up the room in Shenzhen and drive back to Zhanjiang with two drones in the car.
options.end: You became the head of a spraying crew, checking the wind at the edge of the cane fields at dawn and finishing the first field before the sun is up. Your parents say you're as sunburned now as when you delivered food.

options.label: Stay in Shenzhen
options.result: You say your child goes to school here and you can't leave. Your cousin says then come back at New Year and fly a couple of days for me, and you say sure.

options.label: Take two months off in the busy season to help
options.result: Every year in sugarcane spraying season you take two months off, go back to Zhanjiang and fly with your cousin's crew, then return to Shenzhen. People in both places say you've lost weight.

endings.retire: On your last day you go up to the roof once more. The yellow circle on the pad has faded and been repainted many times; the drones take off and land on their own, with only one young man standing beside them. You catch one for him, take off the cargo box and pull the battery to check its temperature. He says leave it to me, Master, and you say fine, and hand him the battery.
endings.burnout: That summer, sitting at the monitoring desk, everything goes black for a moment. The doctor says it's exhaustion, on top of the old back injury, and tells you to stop watching screens on night shifts. The company moves you to writing training materials, compiling the emergency cases from all these years. The first one you write down is those dozen seconds of lost link.

stages: You keep the landing pad on the roof, the one with the yellow circle painted on it. Each time a drone lands you take off the cargo box, swap the battery, check the blades, scan the next order onto it and step behind the yellow line to report ready; in the gaps you log flights and alerts in the handover book. The person at the monitoring desk calls you on the radio, you answer and do the thing, and how the drone flies is not your business.

You sit at the monitoring desk now, flying three or four routes on your own at once. Before each shift you check the weather and set the go/no-go criteria, then watch every drone's battery, track and link on the ground control station. When an alert comes, return, hover or forced landing is your order to give, by the playbook. The people on the pad call you Captain, and for the first time you answer for drones someone else launched.

What you manage now isn't drones but routes. By day you lead a shift of pilots in front of the big monitoring screen, watching on-time rates and alerts; every few days you go survey a new landing site, dealing with property managers, the subdistrict office and the airspace authorities, handing in the applications one by one. On the day a new route flies its trials you stand on the pad, and the signature is yours.

Your day starts with the safety report: how many flights yesterday, how many alerts, how many complaints. You do the roster for the whole center, review training plans, handle certification reviews and insurance renewals, and when regulators inspect, you walk them through item by item. You rarely touch a controller anymore; what you hold is rosters and incident reviews.

What you draw now is the route network for the whole region: which districts need landing sites, which corridors to share with other operators, how to bring in hospitals, logistics parks and government projects. Half your week is meetings and partnership talks, and now and then you speak at an industry forum. Back at the operations center, you still look out the window at the wind first.
work: The person at the monitoring desk says on the radio that drone three's battery is draining fast. After you catch it you pull that battery, put a red tag on it, drop it in the isolation box and write a line in the battery log.

A woman who's come to collect her food can't work the pickup locker, and scans the code wrong three times. You come down from the roof, find her order, and holding her bag of steamed buns she says she'll keep ordering by drone.

Old Liu from maintenance teaches you to listen to propellers: a good one sounds flat, a cracked one gives a faint whine. That afternoon you actually hear one, take it off, and there's a hairline crack at the root.

At four in the afternoon the radar shows a convective cloud moving toward Nanshan. You recall all four drones in the air ten minutes early, and as the last one touches down, the first drop of rain hits the pad.

Midway along a route a drone receives a temporary no-fly notice. You edit the waypoints by hand on the ground station to go around the area, and it arrives six minutes late without the customer noticing a thing.
A new landing-pad operator doesn't latch a cargo box properly. You see it wobble slightly on the monitoring feed, stop the launch at once, and have him latch it again before it goes.

You take a drone and a laser rangefinder to survey a new landing site beside an urban village. The property manager asks whether it's noisy and whether things fall off; you answer point by point and leave him a noise test report.

At the monthly review you put a route's three-month on-time curve on the screen and show that it dips every Thursday afternoon, because the drones have to detour around a nearby school at dismissal time.

The airspace authority sends back one of your route applications, asking for emergency landing sites to be added. You mark five open spaces on the map, photograph each and write a description, and the second time it's approved.

The insurer comes to renew and wants to raise the premium based on last year's incident record. You lay out the handling record for every alert and talk it through, and in the end the rate goes up only a little.

A pilot has failed to fill in his flight log properly three times running. You call him into your office, don't dock his pay, and have him complete a month of logs page by page while you sit with him.

Regulators come for the annual inspection and ask to see the battery management system. You take them to the charging room and scan the batteries one by one; the log matches what's on the shelves, and the inspection form gets a tick.

A top-tier (Grade 3A) hospital wants to hand you sample transport between its campuses. You go four times to negotiate the plan, and in the end, in the clause on safety liability in the partnership agreement, you change seven characters.
Two delivery companies' routes cross above the river channel. You and the other company's head draw up a shared corridor map together, each side's drones flying in staggered time slots.

The AI planning system produces a layout of landing sites for a new district. You walk it on site with two supervisors and strike three of them: one under high-voltage lines, two at the gates of primary schools.
past: You finish middle school in the countryside outside Zhanjiang, an average student whose favorite thing is taking the family radio apart. Your father says go to vocational school and learn to fix cars, and you'll always have a living in the city.
After vocational school in auto repair you follow a classmate to Shenzhen and apprentice at a repair shop, a little over ¥2,000 a month, sleeping in the loft above the shop.
The repair shop closes. You buy a secondhand e-bike and start delivering food, and in your first month you learn every street and alley of Nanshan.
You become one of the top three riders at your station by order count. Your back starts to give you trouble, and riding in winter rain makes your knees ache badly.

One noon in winter, waiting for an order at a park gate, you see a drone land on a pickup locker, four cups of milk tea without a drop spilled. You watch for ten minutes, then look up how to get a license.
You take the visual-line-of-sight license course while still delivering, theory classes at night, practice on weekends. The day you pass, you send a photo of the license to your mother.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Shenzhen's basic pension for company employees, paid on and off as a gig worker in your delivery years and later on the company's wage base, comes to about forty percent of your final monthly pay.
scenes: In your first month of retirement you still check the wind speed first thing in the morning. Four meters a second, and you say it's a good day. Your wife asks, good for whom.
The neighborhood youth center asks you to run a drone club once a week. The first thing you teach the kids is to turn each propeller and feel for cracks.

Your daughter is at university in another city. You order dim sum from around the corner on your phone, and a drone sets it down in the locker downstairs. You go down to collect it, and check its blades while you're there.

On a trip back to Zhanjiang you stand at the edge of a cane field watching a spraying drone skim low over the ground. You tell the young man next to you that if the wind gets any stronger, it can't fly.
No more night shifts. You come home on time every day and cook. Your back gets a little better, you start walking around the estate, and when you see a drone overhead you no longer count its flights.
A young pilot in command at the operations center calls: one route keeps losing link at the same spot. You tell him to go see if a new building has gone up there. He calls back: it has.
When the time comes you retire. Your book of emergency cases is still used in the company's training, and the last page is in your hand: think it through before you launch.
In the first year away from the delivery routes, whenever you hear a hum overhead you stop and look up to see which way it's heading.
You find your footing in the new place. Passing that mall in Nanshan now and then, you see the landing pad on the roof is still there, with several times more drones than in your day.
The little boy who used to wait for drones by the pickup locker later studies drone technology. He finds you online and says that day you let him touch a propeller.
Later there are more and more drones in the sky, and people stop looking up. Only you know that behind every one of them, someone is watching the wind.
Your grandson asks if you used to fly planes. You say yes, planes with nobody in them, carrying milk tea and steamed buns. He thinks that's even better than flying a big plane.

closing.retire: Many years later, walking by the sea one evening, a drone passes overhead on its way to a pickup locker by the water. You stop and watch it land, and the sound of its rotors is as flat as you remember.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find the landing pad's reflective vest in a cupboard, its fluorescent yellow faded pale. You fold it neatly and put it back where it was.
closing.end: Many years later, on a rainy night, you think of the landing pad on that roof, and of the last drone down before a thunderstorm. You don't tell anyone. You just close the window a little.
